title: Customisations
text:
Customisations
Customisations provide a way to adapt this template to your specific requirements and constraints. This section describes a few common customisations that can be applied to the starter project

Adding Secret Variables to Project Files
Changing Materialization for the Staging Layer
Replacing DuckDB with a Cloud Data Warehouse
Replacing Pixi with tox + uv

Additional entries may be added here over time.
Adding Secret Variables to Project Files
The project does not currently require environment variables in dbt_project.yml. If your project needs to access secrets, such as cloud storage credentials, environment variables can be used to keep those values outside the project files.
There are several ways to provide environment variables to dbt. The approach below uses a .env file as the source of the variables and then loads those variables into the environment before dbt runs. The example uses DuckDB’s Secrets Manager to provide credentials for accessing an AWS S3 bucket. DuckDB supports S3 secrets through CREATE SECRET, including credentials supplied through KEY_ID, SECRET, ACCOUNT_ID, and REGION.






WarningSecurity Note



Do not commit credentials or other secrets to version control. If you use a .env file containing secrets, add it to .gitignore.


Adding a .env File
Create a .env file in your home directory (~/.env) and add the required credentials
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<my-aws-access-key>
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<my-aws-secret-access-key>
AWS_ACCOUNT_ID=<my-aws-account-id>
AWS_REGION=<my-aws-region>
The .env file is only the storage location for these values. The variables must be loaded into the process environment before dbt or DuckDB can access them.
Modifying dbt_project.yml
Add an on-run-start hook to dbt_project.yml that creates a DuckDB S3 secret using the environment variables
on-run-start:
  - "CREATE OR REPLACE SECRET (
      TYPE S3,
      KEY_ID '{{ env_var('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID') }}',
      SECRET '{{ env_var('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY') }}',
      ACCOUNT_ID '{{ env_var('AWS_ACCOUNT_ID') }}',
      REGION '{{ env_var('AWS_REGION') }}'
    );"
The env_var() function retrieves the corresponding values from the environment in which dbt is running. DuckDB then uses those values when creating the S3 secret.
Loading .env Variables for Ad-Hoc dbt Commands
For ad-hoc dbt commands, the variables can be loaded from ~/.env before the dbt command is executed. In pyproject.toml, modify the dbt-cmd task for the dbt feature so that the .env variables are loaded into the command environment.
For example
dbt-cmd = { cmd = """
   env $(cat ~/.env | xargs) dbt {{ command }}
   """, description="""\
   Execute adhoc dbt command\
   """, args = ["command"], cwd = ".", default-environment = "dbt" }
The existing dbt-cmd task can then continue to be invoked through Pixi
pixi run dbt-cmd "debug"
This approach makes the variables available to dbt for the duration of the command without requiring them to be defined globally in the user’s shell.
Loading .env Variables for Prefect
The Prefect orchestration flow runs dbt commands from Python rather than directly from the shell. For this workflow, the python-dotenv package is used to load the .env file into the Python process environment. This package is already present in the orchestration feature in pyproject.toml. Additionally, the .env file at ~/Documents/.env is already loaded by the Python script by default
# dbt_orchestrator.py
from pathlib import Path

from dotenv import load_dotenv


PROJ_ROOT = Path.cwd()

assert load_dotenv(
    dotenv_path=PROJ_ROOT.parents[1] / "Documents" / ".env", override=False
)
So, the only modification required is to change the default location of the .env file to ~/.env. To do this, replace
dotenv_path=PROJ_ROOT.parents[1] / "Documents" / ".env", override=False
by
dotenv_path=Path.home() / ".env", override=False
load_dotenv() reads the variables from the specified .env file and adds them to os.environ, making them available to the dbt commands executed by the Prefect flow. Note that, by default, existing environment variables are not overwritten.
Changing Materialization for the Staging Layer
By default, the project’s dbt_project.yml configures models in the staging layer to be materialized as views
models:
  dbt_prefect_starter:
    staging:
      +materialized: view
If, for example, you want the staging layer to write its output to a compressed Parquet file in an AWS S3 bucket, you can change the materialization configuration to
models:
  dbt_prefect_starter:
    staging:
      +materialized: external
      +format: 'parquet'
      +location: "s3://{{ env_var('AWS_BUCKET_NAME') }}/path/to/file/my_file.parquet.gzip"
      +options:
        overwrite: true
        compression: 'gzip'
This configuration uses the external materialization to write the model output as a Parquet file and enables gzip compression. The S3 location is constructed using the AWS_BUCKET_NAME environment variable.






Caution



The S3 configuration requires credentials to be available to DuckDB when the model runs. Follow the instructions for loading secrets as environment variables using a .env file to configure the required AWS credentials.


Replacing DuckDB with Cloud Data Warehouse
This section covers steps to replace DuckDB with a data warehouse from a cloud provider.
Start by removing the following line from the .gitignore file
local_warehouse.duckdb
We will walk through the use of the following warehouses

Snowflake
BigQuery

Two types of changes will be covered

Project Changes

these are changes to be made locally

Storage and Warehouse Changes

these are changes to be made at the warehouse and/or storage level


Snowflake
Project Changes

Create a .env fileand set Github Secrets with the following
SNOWFLAKE_USER_NAME=...
SNOWFLAKE_USER_PASSWORD=...
SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT_LOCATION=...
SNOWFLAKE_WAREHOUSE=...
SNOWFLAKE_DATABASE=...
SNOWFLAKE_SCHEMA=...
SNOWFLAKE_ROLE=...
Replace the profiles.yml in the root directory of the project with ```text resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/snowflake/profiles.yml
In pyproject.toml replace
duckdb = ">=1.5.5, <2"
dbt-duckdb = ">=1.11.0, <2"
by
snowflake-connector-python = "*"
python-dotenv = "*"
Replace the Python runner script run_sql_query.py in the root of the directory with the script from the following location
resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/snowflake/run_sql_query.py
Replace the model sources.yml from
models/staging/stg_open_data_park_occupancy/_stg_*__sources.yml
with
resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/snowflake/_stg_*__sources.yml
Replace the Github actions file from
./.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml
with
resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/snowflake/.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml

Storage and Warehouse Changes
We will assume the raw data is stored in a private Amazon S3 bucket. Snowflake will return an Access Denied error because it has no credentials to authenticate against your private S3 bucket. To fix this, you must explicitly configure authentication between Snowflake and AWS.
Snowflake highly recommends using a secure Storage Integration object (via an AWS IAM Role) rather than hardcoding AWS keys.
Below are the changes required to make your private S3 bucket accessible

Go to your AWS IAM Console, create a new IAM Role in AWS and select Custom Trust Policy and paste a placeholder block (we will update this later)
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "*" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
Attach an IAM policy to this role granting permission to access your private S3 bucket
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:GetObject",
        "s3:GetObjectVersion"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket-name/path/to/csv/*"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:ListBucket",
        "s3:GetBucketLocation"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::your-bucket-name"
    }
  ]
}
Copy your newly created Role ARN (e.g., arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake_s3_role)
Create a Storage Integration in Snowflake by runnig this SQL command using an ACCOUNTADMIN role to establish a secure link with AWS
CREATE OR REPLACE STORAGE INTEGRATION s3_private_integration
  TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
  STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake_s3_role'
  STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://your-bucket-name/path/to/csv/')
To prevent unauthorized access, you must next establish the trust relationship between AWS and Snowflake. In order to do this, you must bind your specific Snowflake account identifier to the AWS IAM Role. Run this command in Snowflake to fetch your unique properties
DESCRIBE INTEGRATION s3_private_integration
and record the values for STORAGE_AWS_IAM_USER_ARN and STORAGE_AWS_EXTERNAL_ID.
Go back to your AWS IAM Role, click Trust Relationships, edit it, and update it with the retrieved values
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "AWS": "<STORAGE_AWS_IAM_USER_ARN_VALUE>"
      },
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "sts:ExternalId": "<STORAGE_AWS_EXTERNAL_ID_VALUE>"
        }
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
    }
  ]
}
Create an existing external stage that maps to your cloud bucket URL where the CSV is kept
CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE my_databasepark_occupy_db.raw_schema.raw_park_occupancy_stage
  URL = 's3://your-bucket-name/path/to/csv/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_private_integration; -- Added authentication
Execute the macro to render and build the object inside Snowflake
pixi run prefect-dbt "run-operation stage_external_sources"
Once staged, it can be queried like any native dbt source. You can run your dbt models as normal
pixi run prefect-dbt "run"

BigQuery
Project Changes

Create a .env file locally and set Github Secrets with the following
BIGQUERY_PROJECT_ID=...
BIGQUERY_DATASET=...
BIGQUERY_LOCATION=...
GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=/path/to/your/service_account_key.json
In Github Secrets, for the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS variable paste the entire raw text content of your service_account.json file here.
Replace dbt’s profiles.yml in the root directory of the project with ```text resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/bigquery/profiles.yml
In pyproject.toml replace
duckdb = ">=1.5.5, <2"
dbt-duckdb = ">=1.11.0, <2"
by
google-cloud-bigquery = "*"
python-dotenv = "*"
Replace the Python runner script run_sql_query.py in the root of the directory with the script from the following location
resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/bigquery/run_sql_query.py
Replace the model sources.yml from
models/staging/stg_open_data_park_occupancy/_stg_*__sources.yml
with
resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/bigquery/_stg_*__sources.yml
Replace the Github actions file from
.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml
with
resources/cloud-dbs-adhoc-sql/bigquery/.github/workflows/deploy-docs.yml

Storage and Warehouse Changes
We will assume the raw data is stored in a private GCS bucket. Because you are using service account authentication via your GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable, the only requirement is to grant that specific service account read access to your private GCS bucket.
Below are the changes required to do this

Identify your Service Account email by opening your service-account.json file specified in your GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable and look for the client_email key. It will look like this
"client_email": "your-service-account@://gserviceaccount.com"
Grant permissions on the private GCS bucket by assigning the Storage Object Viewer (roles/storage.objectViewer) IAM role to this service account on the private bucket. This gives BigQuery the clearance it needs to scan files inside the bucket. This can be done as follows

Using the Google Cloud Console

Go to the Google Cloud Storage Console
Click on your private bucket name (your-toronto-opendata-bucket)
Select the Permissions tab at the top
Click Grant Access (or Add Principal)
In the New principals field, paste your service account’s client_email
In the Select a role dropdown, select Cloud Storage -> Storage Object Viewer
Click Save

using the command line ```bash gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding
gs://
–member=“serviceAccount:your-service-account@://gserviceaccount.com”
–role=“roles/storage.objectViewer”

Once the IAM policy update has propagated, BigQuery can now securely access your private GCS bucket files using the credentials provided in your .env file. You can proceed to deploy and run your external tables normally ```bash pixi run prefect-dbt “run-operation stage_external_sources”
Run your dbt models
pixi run prefect-dbt "run"

Replacing Pixi with tox + uv
Like Pixi, uv is a modern and fast Python package manager that is written in Rust. This project provides readymade configuration files for using uv with tox.
First, move the appropriate files into place

Delete the following files in the root directory of the project

pyproject.toml
Makefile
.gitignore

Move the following files into the root directory

resources/py-env-tools/tox/using-uv/TOML/tox.toml
resources/py-env-tools/tox/using-uv/TOML/Makefile
resources/py-env-tools/tox/using-uv/.gitignore
resources/py-env-tools/tox/using-uv/pyproject.toml








Note



A backup copy of the deleted files required for using Pixi is available in the resources folder

resources/py-env-tools/pixi/pyproject.toml
resources/py-env-tools/pixi/Makefile
resources/py-env-tools/pixi/.gitignore

so if they are deleted they are not lost forever!


Next, install uv
make uv-install-upgrade
which will run
pip3 install --upgrade uv
Next, use uv to install tox using the tox-uv plugin
make uv-install-tox
which runs
uv tool install tox --with tox-uv
Finally, create the uv lockfile (uv.lock) using
uv lock
in order to pin dependencies in uv.lock but it does not pin Python package dependencies in pyproject.toml. This is similar to
pixi upgrade
which creates pixi.lock but also pins Python packages in pyproject.toml.
Now, you can run make rules as normal, since they have the same names as those using Pixi.

title: Opinions
text:
Opinions
Project Organization
In order to follow dbt’s best practices for project structure, the project organization starts with the defaults provided during project initialisation using dbt init.
After initialising a new dbt project, the models/example directory is removed, but otherwise the default structure is kept unchanged. The intention is to provide enough structure to make the project immediately usable without imposing a particular modeling methodology.
While different projects may organize their models in different ways, a staging layer is a common starting point for transforming source data into a consistent form. For this reason, the template includes a small staging model example in the models/staging directory.
The example staging model is organized in its own subdirectory. The associated sources.yml, schema.yml, and SQL files follow a consistent naming convention that makes their purpose and relationship to the model clear. For example, for a model named <model-name> located under models/staging/<model-name>, the source definition and model files would follow the pattern _stg_<model-name>__sources.yml and _stg_<model-name>__records.sql respectively in order to follow dbt’s best practices. The leading underscore also keeps these supporting files visually distinct from the model itself.
Standalone repository
A dbt project can be organized as either a standalone repository or as part of a dbt monorepo. A standalone repository contains a single independent dbt project, while a monorepo can contain multiple dbt projects alongside other related code and resources.
This template uses a standalone repository design. Since its purpose is to provide a starting point for an individual dbt project, keeping the dbt project in its own Git repository keeps the scope and project boundaries clear.
A monorepo may be appropriate when multiple dbt projects need to be managed together, but that additional organizational structure is outside the scope of this starter project.
Python Virtual Environments at the Root of Everything
Reproducibility starts with the computational environment in which the project runs. This project aims to have every part of the workflow - including just running individual dbt commands - to execute within a defined Python environment whose dependencies could be recreated reliably. Python package management was therefore treated as a foundational part of this starter project rather than something left to an individual developer to configure.
The goal is simple that a new user should be able to recreate the environment used to develop and run the project without having to determine which packages, versions, or dbt adapters were installed.
For Python dependency management, this project uses Pixi by default, with the combination of tox and uv provided as an alternative. Both approaches allow the project’s dependencies and environment configuration to be captured in files that can be committed to version control. With Pixi, this configuration is specified in pyproject.toml. For tox and uv, it is defined through tox.ini. This makes the environment part of the project itself rather than a collection of undocumented local setup steps for the user to execute one at a time.
The same principle applies when running dbt commands outside of an orchestrated workflow. For example, an ad hoc command such as dbt deps should execute in the project’s defined environment, where dbt-core and the required database adapter, such as dbt-duckdb, are already installed. This keeps interactive development, automated workflows, and orchestrated pipelines aligned in terms of their dependency definitions and it reduces the risk of a command working on one machine but failing on another.
Ad-Hoc dbt Commands
Running ad-hoc dbt commands quickly is essential for maintaining momentum and accuracy during data development. When building or debugging data pipelines, users frequently need to test small changes, inspect intermediate models, or run specific tests without waiting for the entire project to compile and execute. Prompt execution of commands like dbt run --select my_model or dbt test provides immediate feedback, allowing you to catch syntax errors, logic flaws, or data quality issues in real time.
This rapid iteration cycle minimizes context switching, reduces development friction, and ensures that you can prototype data models fast. It lowers the barrier to entry and supports following best practices from the beginning. This template supports running fast ad-hoc dbt commands out of the box.
In this project, an adhoc dbt command runs in an environment pre-configured using Pixi. So, the user does not have to waste time wrestling with missing dependencies or sluggish execution environments just to run a single model.
Ultimately, supporting ad-hoc dbt commands prevents this starter project from becoming a bottleneck as the project grows.
DAG for End-to-End dbt Pipelines
A dbt project is more than a collection of individual commands. In practice, a complete workflow often consists of multiple dbt operations that need to be executed in a particular order. The dbt CLI executes one command at a time, so commands that are part of a larger workflow must be composed using a shell script, task runner, orchestration tool, or some other mechanism. For example, a workflow may require dependencies to be installed before building models, or may need to generate documentation after the project has been built.
The important distinction is between running a sequence of commands and defining a workflow that manages that sequence. A simple shell command such as
dbt deps && dbt build
can execute two commands in succession. However, as a workflow becomes more complex, it becomes useful to explicitly define the dependencies between its steps and provide a mechanism for executing, monitoring, and retrying those steps.
Scenarios for Sequential Execution of Commands
There are several situations where a dbt workflow may involve multiple distinct commands. Below are some examples.
Checking source freshness before a build
Source freshness can be evaluated separately from the build when freshness is an explicit prerequisite for downstream processing








flowchart LR
  A[dbt soruce freshness] ==> B(dbt build)








Figure 1: Only run dbt build after checking source freshness.



Unlike a simple sequence of dbt commands, a workflow here can use the result of the freshness check to determine whether the subsequent build should proceed at all.
Generating documentation
Documentation generation is another distinct dbt operation that may be part of a larger workflow








flowchart LR
  A[dbt build] ==> B(dbt docs generate)








Figure 2: Generating dbt documentation after running dbt build.



The build establishes the current state of the project and its database objects, after which dbt docs generate can produce the artifacts used to serve the dbt documentation site.
Managing snapshots and downstream models
Snapshots may also be treated as a distinct stage when a workflow needs to capture changes in source data before building downstream models








flowchart LR
  A[dbt snapshot] ==> B(dbt build)








Figure 3: Take a dbt snapshot before running dbt build.



The important point in each of these examples is not that dbt cannot execute the individual operations. It is that a complete data workflow may contain several operations whose order and success criteria need to be managed together.
Why Use an Orchestration Tool?
Running sequential dbt commands from a terminal or shell script is useful for simple workflows, but it leaves the workflow logic largely in the hands of the user or script executing it. As the workflow grows, additional concerns may emerge

task dependencies
retries
scheduling
logging
visibility into failures

Two important properties of a data modeling workflow are correctness and reproducibility. A model should not only produce the expected results, but should also be possible to rerun using the project’s source files and dependencies without relying on undocumented steps or a particular developer’s local environment. Testing is central to establishing correctness, while explicitly defining the modeling workflow as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) makes the dependencies between transformations clear and provides a reproducible execution path.
This is where orchestration becomes important. Ad-hoc dbt commands remain useful for development, but the complete workflow has a repeatable path that can be executed reliably whenever needed.
Data orchestration is the process of scheduling, running, and monitoring open-source dbt Core jobs in production. Unlike dbt Cloud, which includes a built-in scheduler to do this, dbt Core is a command-line tool. That means we need an external orchestrator to handle dependencies, run triggers, retry failed tasks, and alert your team when things break
An orchestration tool provides a layer around the individual dbt operations. Instead of thinking of the workflow as a list of dbt commands to execute, each operation becomes a task with defined dependencies and execution state. This makes the workflow easier to automate, observe, and re-run.
This distinction is important for this starter project.






Important



The purpose of adding an orchestrator is not to replace dbt’s own capabilities or to make a small local project unnecessarily complex. It is to capture how dbt commands can participate in a broader orchestrated workflow while keeping those commands themselves unchanged.


Prefect as the Orchestration Layer
There are many tools for orchestrating workflows and representing DAGs, including Airflow, Luigi, Snakemake, Prefect, and Dagster. This project uses Prefect together with its dbt integration because it provides a Python-native way to define and execute workflows while keeping the dbt project itself independent of the orchestration layer.
In this template, individual dbt operations are represented as Prefect tasks within a Prefect flow. The relationship between Prefect tasks is explicitly defined, and Prefect manages their execution state.
The resulting workflow is more than a sequence of terminal commands. Prefect provides a defined workflow for executing dbt commands and their dependencies, while also making that workflow available through simple project entry points. The result is a pipeline that can be run interactively during development or from a clean state when reproducibility needs to be verified.






ImportantPrefect Cloud Benefits for dbt



Here, we are using Prefect Cloud’s Free Tier which offers some key benefits for a dbt project

No infrastructure to maintain

Prefect handles the scheduling, user interface, and cloud-hosted control plane, which eliminates the need for you to self-host Prefect Server or configure dedicated worker infrastructure for light workloads.

Free serverless compute

The Free Tier includes free monthly serverless execution minutes (typically 500 minutes) to run your dbt flows directly in Prefect’s cloud environment. Prefect’s hybrid architecture means that you get the following privacy benefits

Your workflows, code, and data stay inside your own private network or cloud account.
The workers in your network poll the Prefect Cloud API for instructions using outbound-only requests. This means Prefect Cloud never opens inbound connections into your network.
Prefect Cloud will only handle the control plane, coordination, and scheduling of your workflows. Your actual data processing never flows through Prefect Cloud servers. Only basic run history, task names, run states, and scheduling information are stored on Prefect Cloud.
If you use Prefect blocks to store credentials, those sensitive values are encrypted at rest using cloud key management services.


Remote observability

You instantly gain a real-time remote dashboard to inspect your workflow run histories, view structured logs, and catch failed dbt tasks or model runs.




As an example, in a simple workflow, a dbt build must complete before a subsequent dbt docs generate operation runs, as shown below








flowchart LR
  A[dbt build] ==> B(dbt docs generate)








Figure 4: A simple dbt workflow.



A shell script can express the same dependency with sequential dbt commands. Prefect adds additional workflow capabilities around that dependency

Task dependencies

With dbt, a user can handle this sequence through shell commands or a CI/CD workflow pipeline, rather than inside dbt’s native configuration files. However, a Prefect workflow can explicitly define that a downstream task (docs generate) depends on the successful completion of an upstream task (build). If the upstream task fails, then the dependent task does not proceed as though the prerequisite had succeeded.

Visibility

Prefect provides a graphical user intergace for inspecting workflow runs, task states, execution times, and logs. This makes it easier for a user to determine which step failed without having to reconstruct the execution history from the terminal output. dbt’s native visibility dashboards, timing charts, and job monitoring tools belong exclusively to dbt Cloud and not to dbt core that we are using in this project.

Scheduling and automation

A Prefect flow can be scheduled to run automatically or triggered by external events. This allows the same workflow used during development to become the basis for an automated pipeline when that becomes useful. The dbt scheduler is not available for dbt core which is used here.

Retries and handling failures

Individual tasks can be configured with retry behavior. For example, a transient database connection failure does not necessarily need to cause the entire workflow to be considered permanently failed. Prefect can retry the affected task according to its configuration. You can move beyond basic time-based cron scheduling by using event-driven triggers, retries, and custom logic to kick off your dbt jobs. Here, the retries are set to zero by default, but can be easily changed in the Python source code.


The result is a useful separation of responsibilities. dbt defines the data transformation logic, while Prefect manages the execution of that workflow.
The dbt project remains a normal dbt project, but its commands can also participate in a larger, observable, repeatable DAG when the project needs one.






NoteTesting Prefect Tasks and Flows





Motivation
Unit testing Prefect flows and tasks is critical because it isolates your data engineering logic from network fluctuations, external databases, and live infrastructure dependencies.
By forcing code to execute against an ephemeral, in-memory API, we can validate that task interactions, error-handling retries, and data type schemas behave exactly as designed before deploying code to production. This practice catches logical errors or configuration drifts early in a CI/CD pipeline, drastically reducing debugging times, preventing corrupted datasets, and saving on costly orchestration compute fees.
Implementation Overview
In order to test Prefect 3.x flows and tasks effectively with pytest, the best practice is to isolate the orchestration logic by running against an ephemeral, in-memory API and database.
Pytest has become the industry-standard Python testing framework because it replaces boilerplate code with simple, native assert statements and offers a flexible, modular fixture system that scales effortlessly from tiny scripts to massive codebases. A conftest.py file serves as a centralized configuration hub for a directory, allowing you to define reusable fixtures, plugins, and hooks that are automatically recognized by pytest without needing explicit imports in your test files. Using conftest.py drastically cleans up a test suite by keeping structural setup code, like spinning up an ephemeral Prefect test harness, mocking global database connections, or loading environment variables. This entirely separated from the actual test logic.
In Prefect tests, using a conftest.py file allows for defining a session-scoped fixture that sets up an isolated testing environment once for the entire test suite. This prevents tests from slowing down or writing data to a production Prefect instance.
In this template, a conftest.py was created in the root of the src/tests/ directory. The prefect_test_harness utility was used to spin up the mock backend. Setting scope="session" and autouse=True ensures the harness runs once for all tests, saving significant execution time.
# tests/conftest.py

import pytest
from prefect.testing.utilities import prefect_test_harness


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True, scope="session")def prefect_api_harness():
    """
    Spins up an isolated, ephemeral Prefect API and database 
    once for the entire test session.
    """
    # Increase the startup timeout if your CI environment is slow
    with prefect_test_harness(server_startup_timeout=60):
        yield
Because the fixture in conftest.py is configured with autouse=True, every test in the suite automatically executes within the isolated test harness. We do not need to import or explicitly pass the fixture into the test functions.
With this setup, tests were written in two Python scripts following the naming convention test_*.py and placed in src/tests

test_prefect_tasks.py tests Pefect tasks
test_prefect_flows.py tests the Pefect flow

In order to avoid confusion with the dbt tests folder, Prefect tests were placed alongside the Prefect module code. This is one of the popular test layouts in the Python ecosystem.



Choosing Make as the Project’s Task Runner
make was chosen as the project’s task runner because it is widely available across operating systems and is commonly pre-installed on Unix-based systems. It provides a simple and familiar interface for defining named entry points that execute one or more shell commands.
One benefit of using make as a thin layer over this project’s workflows is that the entry points can remain the same even as the underlying dbt project changes. For example, model directories can be added, removed, or reorganized and dbt_project.yml can change over time without necessarily requiring changes to be made to the Makefile. Similarly, the Python environment used to execute the commands is managed separately using Pixi in pyproject.toml. Make just calls Pixi tasks defined in this file without knowing of any changes that might be made to it.
This keeps the interface for common project operations simple while allowing the user to change implementation underneath it as required.






NoteAnatomy of Makefile Rules Used here





A make rule is a definition in the Makefile that associates a target with the commands that should be executed when that target is invoked. As an example
abc:
    @echo "+ $@"
    @echo "some text"
.PHONY: abc
This rule has three main components

Target (abc)

this is the name used to invoke the rule and, in this example, the name abc represents an action to be performed

Prerequisites (none)

no prerequisites are listed after the colon here, so the rule does not depend on any files or other targets

Recipe (the @echo lines)

these are the shell commands that are executed when the target is invoked


The .PHONY declaration indicates that abc is a command-like target rather than a file that make should consider up to date.
This is useful for task-runner-style Makefiles, where targets represent actions such as running tests, building documentation, or executing a dbt workflow using Prefect.






Tip



Since we are explicitly using make as a task runner here rather than as a traditional compilation/build tool, this walkthrough helps a reader understand why the provided Makefile may look slightly different from the classic make examples found elsewhere.





In this project, each of the two dbt workflows discussed earlier have a corresponding make rule

for running an individual dbt command
for orchestrating a complete dbt workflow with Prefect

Each rule executes within its defined Python environment, so the user does not need to remember the underlying environment activation or command sequence.
Running a workflow is as simple as
make <RULE-NAME>
In this way, the Makefile acts as a small, stable interface to the project’s development workflows. It is not intended to replace dbt or Prefect. Instead, it provides convenient entry points for invoking their commands reproducibly.

title: Documenting and Testing dbt Models
text:
Documenting and Testing dbt Models
Data models are easier to use and maintain when their purpose, columns, and expected behavior are clearly documented and tested. In this starter project, documentation and testing are treated as part of authoring a model rather than as separate tasks performed after the model has been built.
The template uses dbt documentation, column-level tests, and dbt-checkpoint hooks to make these practices consistent across the project. The following conventions describe how models and sources are documented and tested in this starter project.
Documentation Requirements
Each model and source should provide enough metadata for another developer or data consumer to understand what the data represents.
Model Descriptions
Each model should have a top-level description directly below its name in the schema configuration. The description should explain the purpose of the model and, where useful, its grain and the type of transformation it performs.
For example
models:
  - name: _stg_my_model__records
    description: '{{ doc("my_model_description") }}'
Column Descriptions
Every column should have a description in the relevant schema.yml or sources.yml file. Column descriptions are particularly useful for fields whose meaning cannot be understood from the column name alone.
For source definitions, document the columns provided by the raw source. For models, document the columns produced by the transformation.
Using Markdown for Model Documentation
Long descriptions can make YAML configuration files difficult to read. For this reason, this template stores model and column descriptions in Markdown files and references them from the corresponding YAML files using dbt’s docs blocks.
For staging models, documentation is stored under
models/docs/staging/<model_name>.md
The same pattern can be used for intermediate and mart models
models/docs/intermediate/<model_name>.md
models/docs/marts/<model_name>.md
Example Markdown File
For example, the documentation for _stg_my_model__records could be stored in
models/docs/staging/_stg_my_model__records.md
with the following contents
{% docs my_model_description %}

This staging model cleanses and standardizes raw customer records from
the core transactional database. It deduplicates rows based on the
unique ingestion timestamp.

{% enddocs %}

{% docs column_row_id %}

The unique, auto-incrementing primary key for each staging record.

{% enddocs %}
The named documentation blocks can then be referenced from the model’s schema.yml
version: 2

models:
  - name: _stg_my_model__records
    description: '{{ doc("my_model_description") }}'

    columns:
      - name: row_id
        description: '{{ doc("column_row_id") }}'
This keeps the schema configuration concise while allowing longer descriptions to be maintained separately in Markdown.
Testing Requirements
Documentation describes what a model and its columns are expected to represent. Tests provide a way to validate that the resulting data continues to meet those expectations.
Column-Level Tests
Columns should have appropriate tests to validate their expected properties. Depending on the column, this may include tests for uniqueness, null values, accepted values, relationships, or other data-quality expectations.
The appropriate tests depend on the characteristics of the data. Not every column will require the same type of test, but important assumptions about the data should be represented as tests wherever practical.
Top-Level Structural Tests
This project also uses structural checks to ensure that the expected columns are present in a model. This helps identify changes to an upstream source or transformation that could otherwise propagate to downstream models without being immediately noticed.
These checks complement column-level tests. The column-level tests validate the values in individual columns, while structural checks validate that the expected model structure is still present.
Documenting Tests
Tests should also be given descriptive names and descriptions. Test names use lowercase snake_case, with underscores separating words, and should clearly describe the condition being tested.
For example, the following test verifies that values in the year column are 2025 or later
- name: year
  description: 'Year of the customer record'
  data_tests:
    - dbt_expectations.expect_column_values_to_be_between:
        name: year_must_be_2025_or_later
        description: "Ensures the year is 2025 or later."
        arguments:
          min_value: 2025
A descriptive test name makes failures easier to interpret, while the test description documents the expectation being enforced.
Automated Enforcement with pre-commit and dbt-checkpoint
The project uses pre-commit with dbt-checkpoint to automatically check that these conventions are followed. The configured hooks cover areas such as model and source descriptions, column documentation, model tests, source tests, naming conventions, and other dbt project requirements.
The starter project includes nearly 20 dbt-checkpoint hooks. These checks run locally through the project’s lint workflow and can identify missing documentation or tests before changes are committed. They can also be called manually using
make lint
This provides an automated layer of consistency around the conventions described in this section. Rather than relying entirely on developers to remember each requirement, the project uses automated checks to catch common omissions during development.

title: dbt Starter Template with DuckDB and Prefect
text:
dbt Starter Template with DuckDB and Prefect
A lightweight, beginner-friendly starter template providing a clear foundation for structuring a dbt project.
This template is designed for quickly starting local development of a dbt project and it stays close to best practices for structure and style. DuckDB is used as a file-based data warehouse and Prefect is used for dbt command orchestration.
The folder structure stays close to the default dbt project structure after initialising a dbt project so user customisations should be easy to implement.
Highlights

Project entry points configured with simple Makefile for fast data model building and testing with dbt
Modern Python virtual environment management using Pixi for reproducibility
Lightweight but powerful Python-based unit-tested orchestration using Prefect
Duckdb, an OLAP database solution, serving as the modern data warehouse with an analytics focus and zero infrastructure cost, complex configuration, or cloud credentials required
Github Actions configured to run tests, dbt project linting with pre-commmit and deployment of dbt documentation to Github Pages
Starter staging layer with an open dataset loaded from a CSV using DuckDB
Source code in the github repository dbt_duckdb_prefect_starter







TipGetting Started



Start building now with Quickstart.

title: Quickstart
text:
Quickstart
This quickstart walks you through the minimum steps required to set up the project and run the default dbt workflow.






Note



Modifications to default dbt workflow are possible using the Makefile and pyproject.toml file in the root directory of this project.


Prerequisites

Install the prerequisite system packages for the project. See the Prerequisites section for the complete list of tools to be installed. These tools only need to be installed once and should be available globally on your system.
Setup your Prefect Cloud account. The Hobby tier is free forever and offers generous resource limits for orchestrating dbt using this project.

Get Prefect Cloud Connection Details
Get your Prefect API settings (account id and workspace id) from your Prefect Cloud account

Log in to your Prefect Cloud account
The URL in your browser’s address bar will follow this structure
https://app.prefect.cloud/account/[YOUR-ACCOUNT-ID]/workspace/[YOUR-WORKSPACE-ID]/dashboard
Record your account id and workspace id.
Assemble your Prefect Cloud URL, which is the same as the URL above but without the /dashboard suffix
https://app.prefect.cloud/account/[YOUR-ACCOUNT-ID]/workspace/[YOUR-WORKSPACE-ID]

Next, create a Prefect Cloud API key

click on your Profile Avatar or image in the bottom-left corner
select Settings from the menu
click on API Keys in the settings sidebar
click the + Create API Key (or Generate API Key) button
enter a name for the key and set an expiration date
click Create and copy the key

Next, create a file at ~/.prefect/profiles.toml with your Prefect API key and Prefect API URL from above, with the following contents
active = "cloud"

[profiles.default]

[profiles.local]

[profiles.cloud]
PREFECT_API_KEY = "<your-Prefect-Cloud-api-key-here>"
PREFECT_API_URL = "<your-Prefect-Cloud-url-here>"
You have have now configured Prefect to use Prefect Cloud with your personal Free Tier account to run flows with dbt commands. This Prefect Cloud setup has to only be performed once.
Fork the Repository
On this project’s GitHub repository, click the Fork button in the top-right corner.
Clone the Repository
Copy the URL of the forked repository and clone the project
git clone https://github.com/<your-github-user-name>/dbt_prefect_starter.git
Change into the project directory
cd dbt_prefect_duckdb_starter
All commands are run from this directory.
(Optional) Forked Repostory Secrets
Configure your Prefect Cloud API settings as Github Secrets on your fork
PREFECT_API_URL
and
PREFECT_API_KEY
These will be required to run Prefect flows using Github Actions.
(Optional) Update the Project Environment
Update the Python packages managed by Pixi
make pixi-upgrade
This updates the project’s dependencies and Pixi lockfile (pixi.lock) according to the dependency constraints defined by the project.
Test the dbt Connection
Run the default dbt-cmd rule to verify the dbt connection configuration
make dbt-cmd
By default, this runs
dbt debug
which checks the dbt project and its configured connection to DuckDB.
Run the dbt Workflow
Run the complete dbt workflow using Prefect
make prefect-dbt
The workflow runs the following dbt commands in order
dbt debug
dbt deps
dbt run
dbt test
dbt docs generate
The project is now set up and the default dbt workflow has been executed.
View Flow Run on Prefect Cloud
From the Prefect Cloud dashboard, debug the flow run

click on Flow Runs in the side bar
click on dbt_prefect_starter_flow

this is the name specified in the flow definition

click on an individual flow run to view the operational and status information logged about that run, including

state and status

see the current state such as Running, Completed, or Failed and history

timing

see the start time and total execution duration

parameters

see the exact input parameters passed into the flow run

logs

view the real-time or historical log output captured during execution of the flow

executon graph

view the visual map showing the sequence and status of tasks and upstream dependencies

errors

see any errors that occured during the flow run



Enjoy!

title: Authoring dbt Models
text:
Authoring dbt Models
This starter project includes an example staging model, along with boilerplate structure for intermediate and marts models. The example is intentionally small, but it is documented and tested so that it can serve as a starting point for building additional models.
The goal of this section is not to provide a comprehensive introduction to dbt modeling. Instead, it describes how models are organized and named in this starter project and provides a starting point for adding your own models. For a more detailed explanation of dbt modeling concepts, refer to the dbt documentation.
Staging Model
The example staging model is located in
models/staging/stg_open_data_park_occupancy/
The directory name uses underscores rather than dashes, per dbt best practices for styling. This template uses descriptive directory and model names so that the purpose of a model can be understood from its location and name.
The staging model retrieves raw parking lot occupancy readings from the Toronto Open Data Portal. It is therefore named
_stg_open_data_park_occupancy__records
The model name follows the convention used throughout this template and consists of four parts

Leading underscore

this distinguishes the model file from its supporting files

Prefix (stg)

this identifies the staging layer

Model name (open_data_park_occupancy)

this describes the data represented by the model

Suffix (records)

this describes the type of relation represented by the model


The prefix and model name are separated by a single underscore, while the model name and suffix are separated by a double underscore
_stg_open_data_park_occupancy__records
│    │                       │    |
│    │                       |    └── suffix 
│    └── model name          |
└── layer prefix             └── double underscore
The same general naming pattern is used for models in the other layers, with the prefix indicating the layer.
Supporting Files
The staging model directory contains the model SQL file and two supporting YAML files

a schema file, which documents and tests the model
a sources file, which defines the raw data source

Schema File
The schema file contains a top-level models key. Under the model definition, it provides the model name and description, along with descriptions and tests for the model’s columns.
For this starter project, the schema file is intended to demonstrate a documented model with column-level tests. When adding a new model, follow the same pattern so that the model and its columns are documented and validated consistently.
Sources File
The sources file contains a top-level sources key and defines the raw source used by the staging model. It includes the source name and description, along with column descriptions and tests.
The source definition also contains additional configuration used by this project, including schema, freshness, and meta. Because the example loads raw data from a public CSV file, the URL for the external data is stored under
meta:
  external_location
The sources file is specific to the staging layer because this is where raw source data enters the dbt project. Intermediate and mart models are built from upstream dbt models and therefore do not require their own source definitions.
Intermediate and Mart Models
Intermediate and marts models are defined in the models/intermediate and models/marts directories. These follow the same general approach as the staging layer. Each contains an example model and supporting schema file that demonstrate how the model can be documented and tested.
The template uses the following prefixes for these layers

int for intermediate models
fct for fact models in the marts layer
dim for dimension models in the marts layer

For example, a mart model may use a name such as
_fct_<model_name>__records
or
_dim_<model_name>__records
The fct and dim prefixes provide a simple way to distinguish the two common types of mart models. In general, fact models contain measurements or events, while dimension models contain descriptive attributes about the entities represented in those facts.






NoteMarts Models - fct vs dim





The distinction used by this template is

fct

this stores measurements, metrics, or records of business events

dim

this stores descriptive context and attributes about business entities


These conventions are organizational choices rather than requirements imposed by dbt.



Building New Models
When adding a new model, use the existing example as a template rather than starting from an empty directory. The basic workflow is

Choose the appropriate layer

determine whether the model belongs in staging, intermediate, or marts

Create a descriptive model directory

use lowercase names with underscores

Follow the project’s naming convention

use the appropriate layer prefix and a descriptive model name

Create the model SQL file

add the transformation logic for the new model

Add a schema file

document the model and its columns and add the appropriate tests

Define a source when required

staging models that introduce a new raw data source should define that source in a sources file

Build and test the model

use the project’s existing make rules to run the dbt workflow and verify that the model builds successfully and its tests pass


For example, if a new source contains customer records, the resulting staging directory might follow the same pattern as the example
models/
└── staging/
    └── stg_customer/
        ├── _stg_customer__sources.yml
        ├── _stg_customer__schema.yml
        └── _stg_customer__records.sql
The exact contents of the SQL and YAML files will depend on the data being modeled. The important point is to preserve the project’s separation between source definitions, model logic, and model documentation/tests.






Tip



This structure is intentionally lightweight. As a project grows, additional models, tests, sources, and intermediate transformations can be added without requiring the overall organization of the project to change.

title: Motivation for this project
text:
Motivation for this project
A simple starting point
Getting started with a new project using dbt often involves more setup than actual model development. A beginner user may need to read through documentation for dbt, decide how to manage Python environments, orchestration, and a data warehouse before writing a dbt model. This project provides a working starting point that brings these pieces together in a small, understandable structure.
The goal is to make it easy to get up and running without having to first go through documentation to understand where and when things need to happen. Common tasks have clear entry points. The project structure stays close enough to dbt best practices for structure and style that the organization of the project is largely self-documenting.
The user can quickly start running a dbt pipeline while exploring the project structure or looking up concepts in the extensive dbt documentation.
A reproducible local development environment
The template also provides a foundation for local development in a reproducible manner

Python virtual environments are used to make the project’s dependencies explicit with a modern environment management tool like Pixi used by default
DuckDB provides a local, file-based analytical database without requiring the setup of a cloud data warehouse account
Prefect Cloud provides an orchestration layer that can run individual dbt commands or sequences of commands, giving the project useful but lightweight workflow capabilities such as real-time monitoring and observability in a centralised UI out of the box without requiring a large orchestration platform
Pre-defined make rules provide simple entry points for common dbt tasks, making it easy to return to a project later, re-run a workflow, or iterate quickly during model development.

Together, these pieces provide much of the supporting infrastructure needed for a local dbt project while keeping the focus on developing and testing data models. Being able to focus on dbt data modeling and not on project administration was the most important reason for creating this starter project.
Follow conventions without over-engineering
The project aims to follow established dbt practices without being too opinionated. It provides a sensible structure, conventions, and workflow, but documents the reasoning behind its choices so that users can understand what has been included and decide what they want to keep, change, or remove. The intention is not to create another abstraction layer around dbt, but to provide a small project structure in which the important details remain visible and easy to find.
DuckDB, dbt, Prefect, Python, and other development tools can therefore be used as building blocks instead of as constraints on how a dbt project should be organized in order to follow dbt’s own published best practices.
A starting point, not a framework - Adapt as required
Note that nothing in this template is intended to be binding.
It is meant to be a lightweight starting structure that can be adapted to suit the needs of an individual project. The hope is that it provides a useful take-off point for local dbt projects using DuckDB and Prefect Cloud, allowing you (the user) to focus on quickly developing and iterating on data models.
As a project grows, the structure and tooling can be changed as needed.

title: Use This Project
text:
Use This Project
This section provides a guide to the most common tasks you can perform with the project, from cloning the repository to configuring the environment and updating its dependencies.






ImportantAssumptions



We assume herre that your have installed the required pre-requisite system packages have been installed and that the Prefect Cloud credentials are stored in ~/.prefect/profiles.toml.


Fork the Project on Github
Fork the repository to create a personal, independent copy of it on your GitHub account. This gives you full control to modify the code to suit your needs without affecting the original project. This gives you a foundation to build upon rather than starting from scratch.
(Optional) Set Secrets for Forked Repository
In order to run Prefect flows using Prefect Cloud as part of Github Actions, you will need to configure your forked repository with your Prefect Cloud secrets. To do so, set the following two secrets
PREFECT_API_URL
and
PREFECT_API_KEY
See the Quickstart section for steps to extract these values from your Prefect Cloud account.
Cloning the Project
If git is installed, then clone the forked repository with the following
git clone https://github.com/<your-github-user-name>/dbt_prefect_duckdb_starter.git
This is a standalone dbt project, so there is no additional repository or project directory to navigate. Change into the project’s root directory
cd dbt_prefect_duckdb_starter
From the project root, the project’s make rules provide convenient entry points for running dbt commands and workflows. Later, we’ll talk more about the make rules available to you.
Set the Time Zone
The project uses the dbt-expectations package, which requires a time zone to be specified. The default value can be changed in dbt_project.yml
vars:
  'dbt_date:time_zone': 'America/New_York'
The value should be a time-zone identifier recognized by the IANA Time Zone Database, also known as the tz or zoneinfo database. IANA identifiers generally follow an Area/Location format.
Some commonly used values include

Global

UTC
GMT

North America

America/New_York
America/Chicago
America/Denver
America/Los_Angeles
America/Phoenix
America/Toronto

Europe

Prefer canonical IANA identifiers over abbreviations such as EST, CST, or PST. These abbreviations can be ambiguous and may not adequately represent daylight-saving transitions. For example, CST can refer to Central Standard Time but also to China Standard Time.
Legacy identifiers such as US/Eastern and US/Pacific are also best avoided when a canonical identifier such as America/New_York or America/Los_Angeles is available.
DuckDB and Time Zones
The project’s DuckDB environment supports time-zone functionality through DuckDB’s built-in ICU extension. The project also uses DuckDB through Python for running ad-hoc SQL queries.
For the standard project setup, no additional configuration is required beyond changing the dbt_date:time_zone value in dbt_project.yml. DuckDB’s Python integration includes the required functionality, while the DuckDB CLI can automatically load the ICU extension when needed.
(Optional) Upgrade Python Packages
To update the project’s Pixi-managed Python packages, run
make pixi-upgrade
This updates the project’s dependency lockfile and manifest file (pyproject.toml) according to the package constraints defined by the project. Using Pixi to manage the environment keeps dependency resolution and package versions captured as part of the project rather than relying on packages installed independently on a developer’s machine.
Upgrading the manifest file is optional so it is not necessary to run this command.
About Python Virtual Environments
As mentioned above, by default, this project uses Pixi to manage its Python environments and dependencies. Pixi is configured through pyproject.toml, which is committed to the repository so that the project’s environments, dependencies, and tasks are defined alongside the rest of the code.
The pyproject.toml file uses three related Pixi concepts

Feature dependencies

these define the Python packages and other dependencies required by a particular area of the project
this project has separate features for dbt, orchestration, and linting

Environments

one or more features can be combined into an environment in Pixi
an environment therefore provides the complete set of dependencies and tasks needed for a particular workflow

Feature tasks

these define commands that can be executed using the dependencies provided by their feature
here, these tasks include dbt commands, Python scripts, and linting commands


Keeping these concerns separate makes the project’s environments modular. A feature only needs to declare the dependencies relevant to its own functionality. By comparison, a Pixi environment can combine features when a workflow requires functionality from more than one area.
We’ll see how these concepts are used in this project to ensure reproducibility.
Project Features
The project defines three dbt-related Pixi features

dbt
orchestration
lint

The dbt feature contains the dependencies required to work with dbt and DuckDB. Because DuckDB is the project’s data warehouse, this includes the duckdb and dbt-duckdb (the dbt adapter) packages.
The orchestration feature contains the dependencies required to run the Python script that uses Prefect to orchestrate dbt commands. Its environment also includes the dependencies from the dbt feature because the Prefect workflow ultimately executes dbt.
The lint feature contains pre-commit, which is required to run the project’s dbt-checkpoint hook. Its environment also includes the dependencies from the dbt feature so that the linting workflow has access to the dbt project and its associated tooling.
The environments are named either the same as their corresponding feature or according to the workflow they represent






Feature
Environment




dbt
dbt


orchestration
prefectdbt


lint
lint





Table 1: Relationship between features and environments in Pixi configuration file.



This gives each workflow a focused environment while allowing environments to compose the dependencies they need from multiple features.
Pixi Tasks
The environments provide the dependencies, while Pixi tasks provide convenient commands for using them. This project defines tasks for three main workflows.
Workflow 1 - dbt
The dbt feature provides two tasks
Task 1 - dbt-cmd
This task runs an ad-hoc dbt command in the dbt environment. The dbt command itself is supplied as an argument. For example, the following runs dbt test
pixi run dbt-cmd "test"
The corresponding Makefile rule can be used as a shorter entry point
make dbt-cmd
The dbt command passed to the task is configured in the Makefile, so the command can be changed there without changing the Pixi task definition.
Task 2 - adhocsql
This task executes a SQL script against the project’s DuckDB database. The SQL file to execute is supplied as an argument
pixi run adhocsql "analyses/check_parking_occupancy_records.sql"
The Makefile provides a corresponding entry point
make run-adhoc-query
As with dbt-cmd, the SQL file used by the Makefile rule can be changed without modifying the underlying Pixi task.
Workflow 2 - orchestration
The orchestration feature provides the prefect-dbt task. This task runs the Python script responsible for orchestrating dbt commands using Prefect. Because the prefectdbt environment combines the dbt and orchestration features, the workflow has access to both Prefect and dbt.
Multiple dbt commands can be supplied to the task as a comma-separated string. For example
pixi run prefect-dbt "debug,deps,run,test,docs generate"
Again, the same workflow can be invoked through the Makefile
make prefect-dbt
The sequence of dbt commands used by the Makefile rule can be changed there without modifying the Pixi task itself.
Workflow 3 - lint
The lint feature provides the lint task, which runs pre-commit. The project’s pre-commit configuration uses dbt-checkpoint hooks to check aspects of the dbt project’s structure and syntax.
The task can be run directly through Pixi
pixi run lint
or through the Makefile
make lint
How the Pieces Fit Together
The relationship between Pixi features, environments, and tasks can be summarized as follows








flowchart TD
    F1[dbt Feature]
    F2[orchestration Feature]
    F3[lint Feature]

    F1 ==> E1[dbt Environment]
    F1 ==> E2[prefectdbt Environment]
    F2 ==> E2
    F1 ==> E3[lint Environment]
    F3 ==> E3

    E1 ==> T1(dbt Tasks)
    E2 ==> T2(Prefect / dbt Tasks)
    E3 ==> T3(Lint Task)








Figure 1: Features define reusable pieces, while environments compose those features for specific workflows.



For example, the prefectdbt environment combines the dbt and orchestration features. This gives the Prefect workflow access to the dependencies and tasks defined by both features, while keeping the dependency definitions themselves separated by purpose.
This structure also means that the same underlying tasks can be accessed through two levels of interface

directly with pixi run when more control is useful
through the project’s make rules when a simple, predefined entry point is preferred

View Available make Rules
To view all available make rules and their descriptions, run
make help
Each rule includes a short description. Rules that run dbt commands execute within a Python virtual environment managed by Pixi and call the corresponding Pixi task defined in pyproject.toml.
The following make rules provide dbt-related functionality
Available rules:

lint                Run lint checks manually
dbt-cmd             Run ad-hoc dbt command
prefect-dbt         Run dbt commands with Prefect
run-adhoc-query     Run ad-hoc SQL queries with DuckDB
Run Pixi Tasks with make
Running Ad-Hoc dbt Commands
To run a single dbt command within the project’s Pixi-managed Python environment, modify the dbt-cmd rule in the Makefile. By default, the rule is configured to run dbt debug
pixi run dbt-cmd "debug"
For example, to run dbt deps, change the command to
pixi run dbt-cmd "deps"
Then run the make rule
make dbt-cmd
This provides a convenient way to run individual dbt commands without manually activating the Python environment.
Using Orchestration
To run one or more dbt commands through Prefect, modify the prefect-dbt rule in the Makefile. By default, Prefect flow runs the following commands in order with task dependencies as discussed in the Opinions section

dbt debug
dbt deps
dbt run
dbt test
dbt docs generate

The corresponding Pixi task is
pixi run prefect-dbt "debug,deps,run,test,docs generate"
For example, to run dbt test followed by dbt clean, in which the test command must successfully complete, change the command to
pixi run prefect-dbt "test,clean"
Then run the make rule
make prefect-dbt
Prefect executes the specified dbt commands as part of the flow, providing the orchestration layer for their execution.






Tip💡 Extendability of Prefect Flows



In addition to running dbt commands, the Prefect flow was adapted to also clean up the project folder by removing dbt artifacts when using DuckDB. Here, running the dbt command
dbt clean
triggers a Prefect task that cleans up the

file-based data warehouse at local_warehouse.duckdb
__pycache__ folder which is automatically generated by Python to store compiled bytecode

This is a simple example of how Prefect, being a general purpose orchestrator, can be used to perform non-dbt tasks that are essential to a dbt project.
In a similar way, the flow can be extended to perform other non-dbt tasks as you may require!


Code Linting and Validation
The project uses pre-commit with dbt-checkpoint to run a set of checks against the dbt project. The configured hooks can be modified in .pre-commit-config.yaml as needed.
By default, the following dbt-checkpoint hooks are configured

dbt-parse
dbt-docs-generate
check-model-has-properties-file
check-script-semicolon
check-script-has-no-table-name
check-model-has-all-columns
check-model-columns-have-desc
check-model-has-tests
check-model-parents-name-prefix
check-model-has-description
check-source-has-tests
check-source-has-tests-by-type
check-source-has-freshness
check-source-columns-have-desc
check-source-has-description
check-source-table-has-description
check-macro-has-description

To run the configured checks, use
make lint
No changes to the Makefile are required. The lint rule invokes the corresponding Pixi task, which runs the configured pre-commit checks.

title: Contributing
text:
Contributing
This starter project is intentionally opinionated, but it is not intended to be definitive.
The choices made here reflect what works for the project today and may change as dbt, its ecosystem, and our own understanding of best practices evolve. For example, dbt-core is installed as a Python package from PyPI, and the version used by the project will change over time as new releases become available. The dbt core ecosystem is evolving, and this project should evolve with it.
The objective is to make it easier and faster to get started with dbt, work within a well-structured project, and have a basic but complete example that just runs to build from.
If you have suggestions, encounter problems, or have found a better way to approach something, pull requests and issues are strongly encouraged on the repository on Github.
It would be great to hear what works for you, what doesn’t, and what you think could make this starter project more useful.

title: Contributor Covenant 3.0 Code of Conduct
text:
Contributor Covenant 3.0 Code of Conduct
Our Pledge
We pledge to make our community welcoming, safe, and equitable for all.
We are committed to fostering an environment that respects and promotes the dignity, rights, and contributions of all individuals, regardless of characteristics including race, ethnicity, caste, color, age, physical characteristics, neurodiversity, disability, sex or gender, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, language, philosophy or religion, national or social origin, socio-economic position, level of education, or other status. The same privileges of participation are extended to everyone who participates in good faith and in accordance with this Covenant.
Encouraged Behaviors
While acknowledging differences in social norms, we all strive to meet our community’s expectations for positive behavior. We also understand that our words and actions may be interpreted differently than we intend based on culture, background, or native language.
With these considerations in mind, we agree to behave mindfully toward each other and act in ways that center our shared values, including:

Respecting the purpose of our community, our activities, and our ways of gathering.
Engaging kindly and honestly with others.
Respecting different viewpoints and experiences.
Taking responsibility for our actions and contributions.
Gracefully giving and accepting constructive feedback.
Committing to repairing harm when it occurs.
Behaving in other ways that promote and sustain the well-being of our community.

Restricted Behaviors
We agree to restrict the following behaviors in our community. Instances, threats, and promotion of these behaviors are violations of this Code of Conduct.

Harassment. Violating explicitly expressed boundaries or engaging in unnecessary personal attention after any clear request to stop.
Character attacks. Making insulting, demeaning, or pejorative comments directed at a community member or group of people.
Stereotyping or discrimination. Characterizing anyone’s personality or behavior on the basis of immutable identities or traits.
Sexualization. Behaving in a way that would generally be considered inappropriately intimate in the context or purpose of the community.
Violating confidentiality. Sharing or acting on someone’s personal or private information without their permission.
Endangerment. Causing, encouraging, or threatening violence or other harm toward any person or group.
Behaving in other ways that threaten the well-being of our community.

Other Restrictions

Misleading identity. Impersonating someone else for any reason, or pretending to be someone else to evade enforcement actions.
Failing to credit sources. Not properly crediting the sources of content you contribute.
Promotional materials. Sharing marketing or other commercial content in a way that is outside the norms of the community.
Irresponsible communication. Failing to responsibly present content which includes, links or describes any other restricted behaviors.

Reporting an Issue
Tensions can occur between community members even when they are trying their best to collaborate. Not every conflict represents a code of conduct violation, and this Code of Conduct reinforces encouraged behaviors and norms that can help avoid conflicts and minimize harm.
When an incident does occur, it is important to report it promptly. To report a possible violation, please raise an issue on the Github repository.
Community Moderators take reports of violations seriously and will make every effort to respond in a timely manner. They will investigate all reports of code of conduct violations, reviewing messages, logs, and recordings, or interviewing witnesses and other participants. Community Moderators will keep investigation and enforcement actions as transparent as possible while prioritizing safety and confidentiality. In order to honor these values, enforcement actions are carried out in private with the involved parties, but communicating to the whole community may be part of a mutually agreed upon resolution.
Addressing and Repairing Harm
[NOTE: The remedies and repairs outlined below are suggestions based on best practices in code of conduct enforcement. If your community has its own established enforcement process, be sure to edit this section to describe your own policies.]
If an investigation by the Community Moderators finds that this Code of Conduct has been violated, the following enforcement ladder may be used to determine how best to repair harm, based on the incident’s impact on the individuals involved and the community as a whole. Depending on the severity of a violation, lower rungs on the ladder may be skipped.

Warning

Event: A violation involving a single incident or series of incidents.
Consequence: A private, written warning from the Community Moderators.
Repair: Examples of repair include a private written apology, acknowledgement of responsibility, and seeking clarification on expectations.

Temporarily Limited Activities

Event: A repeated incidence of a violation that previously resulted in a warning, or the first incidence of a more serious violation.
Consequence: A private, written warning with a time-limited cooldown period designed to underscore the seriousness of the situation and give the community members involved time to process the incident. The cooldown period may be limited to particular communication channels or interactions with particular community members.
Repair: Examples of repair may include making an apology, using the cooldown period to reflect on actions and impact, and being thoughtful about re-entering community spaces after the period is over.

Temporary Suspension

Event: A pattern of repeated violation which the Community Moderators have tried to address with warnings, or a single serious violation.
Consequence: A private written warning with conditions for return from suspension. In general, temporary suspensions give the person being suspended time to reflect upon their behavior and possible corrective actions.
Repair: Examples of repair include respecting the spirit of the suspension, meeting the specified conditions for return, and being thoughtful about how to reintegrate with the community when the suspension is lifted.

Permanent Ban

Event: A pattern of repeated code of conduct violations that other steps on the ladder have failed to resolve, or a violation so serious that the Community Moderators determine there is no way to keep the community safe with this person as a member.
Consequence: Access to all community spaces, tools, and communication channels is removed. In general, permanent bans should be rarely used, should have strong reasoning behind them, and should only be resorted to if working through other remedies has failed to change the behavior.
Repair: There is no possible repair in cases of this severity.


This enforcement ladder is intended as a guideline. It does not limit the ability of Community Managers to use their discretion and judgment, in keeping with the best interests of our community.
Scope
This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public or other spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official email address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.
Attribution
This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 3.0, permanently available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/3/0/.
Contributor Covenant is stewarded by the Organization for Ethical Source and licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0. To view a copy of this license, visit https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/
For answers to common questions about Contributor Covenant, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are provided at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations. Additional enforcement and community guideline resources can be found at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/resources. The enforcement ladder was inspired by the work of Mozilla’s code of conduct team.
